chunks.text: 3 Methodology 3.1 Problem Formulation We study language-free medical anomaly detection under zero-shot and few-shot settings. Given a query image x ∈ ℝ H × W × 3 x\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} , the goal is to predict an image-level anomaly score s ​ ( x ) s(x) and, when pixel-level annotations are available, an anomaly map 𝐀 ​ ( x ) ∈ ℝ H × W \mathbf{A}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W} . The benchmark contains multiple medical domains { 𝒟 ( j ) } j = 1 J \{\mathcal{D}^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^{J} . In the leave-one-out zero-shot setting, one domain is held out for testing, while the remaining domains form 𝒟 src \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{src}} for source-domain training. In the few-shot setting, a target-domain support set 𝒮 = { ( x i , y i , m i ) } i = 1 N \mathcal{S}=\{(x_{i},y_{i},m_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} is provided, where y i ∈ { 0 , 1 } y_{i}\in\{0,1\} denotes the image-level label and m i m_{i} is the lesion mask when available. ReCAP performs anomaly scoring entirely in the visual feature space using two complementary branches (Figure 1 ). The conditional prototype branch produces an input-specific normal/abnormal boundary, while the few-shot memory branch measures deviations from normal support references. The complete procedure is provided in Appendix A . 3.2 Multi-level Features and Visual Prototypes Multi-level Patch Tokens. We use a frozen CLIP visual encoder and insert lightweight segmentation and detection adapters into selected transformer layers Ω \Omega ( { 6 , 12 , 18 , 24 } \{6,12,18,24\} for ViT-L/14). The segmentation adapter preserves spatially faithful patch features for dense anomaly localization, while the detection adapter produces discriminative patch responses for image-level anomaly scoring. We extract ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -normalized multi-level patch tokens from both adapters and use them for prototype-based scoring. Detailed multi-level patch token extraction is provided in Appendix B.1 . Visual Prototypes.

In place of text embeddings, each branch and layer maintains a normal prototype q l b , n ∈ ℝ C q_{l}^{b,n}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} and abnormal prototype q l b , a ∈ ℝ C q_{l}^{b,a}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} . These prototypes define a base normal/abnormal boundary that is re-centered for each input by the conditional modulation module. In the few-shot setting, the prototypes are initialized from the corresponding normal and abnormal support patch statistics; in the zero-shot setting, source-trained prototypes serve as the base anchors for the unseen target. In both settings, the prototypes are optimized together with the adapters and conditioning modules. Detailed initialization is provided in Appendix B.2 . 3.3 Conditional Prototype Modulation A static prototype is a single point in feature space, yet the optimal normal/abnormal boundary depends on the location of the input. For example, the normal-feature distribution of brain MRI sits far from that of liver CT or retinal OCT. We therefore make the boundary input-conditional and predict it for each image based on its own appearance. Input Context Descriptor. For each branch and layer, we summarize the query into a context descriptor by average-pooling its patch tokens followed by normalization: c l b ​ ( x ) = Norm ⁡ ( 1 R l ​ ∑ r = 1 R l p l , r b ​ ( x ) ) ∈ ℝ C . c_{l}^{b}(x)=\operatorname{Norm}\left(\frac{1}{R_{l}}\sum_{r=1}^{R_{l}}p_{l,r}^{b}(x)\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{C}. (1) This descriptor captures the global appearance of the image, such as its modality and dominant structure, and serves as the conditioning signal. Bounded Gated Modulation.

Each prototype is re-centered by the context through a bounded gated residual: q ~ l b , z = Norm ⁡ ( q l b , z + σ ​ ( β l b , z ) ​ η ​ tanh ⁡ ( W l b , z ​ c l b ​ ( x ) ) ) , \tilde{q}_{l}^{b,z}=\operatorname{Norm}\Big(q_{l}^{b,z}+\sigma(\beta_{l}^{b,z})\,\eta\,\tanh\big(W_{l}^{b,z}\,c_{l}^{b}(x)\big)\Big), (2) where W l b , z ∈ ℝ C × C W_{l}^{b,z}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times C} and β l b , z ∈ ℝ \beta_{l}^{b,z}\in\mathbb{R} are learnable, σ ​ ( ⋅ ) \sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid, and η > 0 \eta>0 is a fixed modulation strength. The bound on this residual is deliberate and specific to anomaly detection. Because c l b ​ ( x ) c_{l}^{b}(x) is pooled over the entire image, on an abnormal input, it is contaminated by the lesion itself. An unconstrained modulation could exploit this by shifting the normal anchor toward the anomalous content, thereby lowering the training loss while making genuine anomalies appear normal at test time. To mitigate this, the learnable gate σ ​ ( β l b , z ) ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \sigma(\beta_{l}^{b,z})\in(0,1) and the bounded tanh \tanh keep the residual small, so that the conditioned anchor q ~ l b , z \tilde{q}_{l}^{b,z} stays close to the learned base prototype. The boundary, therefore, re-centers toward the current domain rather than collapsing onto arbitrary content. As a result, a single set of source-trained prototypes can adapt to an unseen domain in a single forward pass, providing an amortized, gradient-free alternative to test-time adaptation that requires no target labels. Patch-level and Image-level Scoring. For a query patch p ^ l , r b ​ ( x ) \hat{p}_{l,r}^{b}(x) , we form scaled-cosine logits against the conditioned anchors: g l , r b ​ ( x ) = α ​ [ ⟨ p ^ l , r b ​ ( x ) , q ~ l b , n ⟩ , ⟨ p ^ l , r b ​ ( x ) , q ~ l b , a ⟩ ] ∈ ℝ 2 , g_{l,r}^{b}(x)=\alpha\big[\,\langle\hat{p}_{l,r}^{b}(x),\tilde{q}_{l}^{b,n}\rangle,\langle\hat{p}_{l,r}^{b}(x),\tilde{q}_{l}^{b,a}\rangle\,\big]\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, (3) with a fixed logit scale α \alpha .

The patch-level abnormal probability is the abnormal entry of the softmax, a l , r b ( x ) = softmax ( g l , r b ( x ) ) a a_{l,r}^{b}(x)=\operatorname{softmax}\big(g_{l,r}^{b}(x)\big)_{a} . Equivalently, a l , r b ​ ( x ) = σ ​ ( ϕ l , r b ​ ( x ) ) a_{l,r}^{b}(x)=\sigma\big(\phi_{l,r}^{b}(x)\big) with the patch anomaly logit: ϕ l , r b ​ ( x ) = α ​ ( ⟨ p ^ l , r b ​ ( x ) , q ~ l b , a ⟩ − ⟨ p ^ l , r b ​ ( x ) , q ~ l b , n ⟩ ) , \phi_{l,r}^{b}(x)=\alpha\big(\langle\hat{p}_{l,r}^{b}(x),\tilde{q}_{l}^{b,a}\rangle-\langle\hat{p}_{l,r}^{b}(x),\tilde{q}_{l}^{b,n}\rangle\big), (4) which is the normal-versus-abnormal margin under the conditioned boundary. For localization, the segmentation adapter reshapes the two-class patch logits { g l , r seg ​ ( x ) } \{g_{l,r}^{\mathrm{seg}}(x)\} into 2D logit maps and upsamples them to the input resolution. A channel-wise softmax is then applied, and the abnormal channel forms the layer-wise anomaly map. For image-level detection, the patch-level abnormal probabilities { a l , r det ​ ( x ) } \{a_{l,r}^{\mathrm{det}}(x)\} are aggregated using the multi-layer fusion described next. 3.4 Normal-Reference Memory and Layer Fusion Normal-Reference Memory. The conditional prototype branch models normality using a compact re-centered anchor. To retain instance-level normal variation in the few-shot setting, we build a non-parametric memory ℳ l b \mathcal{M}_{l}^{b} from the patch tokens of all normal support images ( y i = 0 y_{i}=0 ). Each query patch is scored by its nearest-neighbor cosine distance: d l , r b ​ ( x ) = min u ∈ ℳ l b ⁡ ( 1 − ⟨ p ^ l , r b ​ ( x ) , u ^ ⟩ ) , d_{l,r}^{b}(x)=\min_{u\in\mathcal{M}_{l}^{b}}\left(1-\langle\hat{p}_{l,r}^{b}(x),\hat{u}\rangle\right), (5) where u ^ \hat{u} is an ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -normalized memory feature.

Since the cosine distance between normalized features lies in [ 0 , 2 ] [0,2] , we map it to the prototype probability range as d ¯ l , r b ​ ( x ) = clip ⁡ ( d l , r b ​ ( x ) 2 , 0 , 1 ) , \bar{d}_{l,r}^{b}(x)=\operatorname{clip}\left(\frac{d_{l,r}^{b}(x)}{2},\,0,\,1\right), (6) where d ¯ l , r b ​ ( x ) \bar{d}_{l,r}^{b}(x) denotes the normalized memory anomaly response used for subsequent layer and branch fusion. Large normalized distances indicate deviations from observed target-domain normal patterns. The memory branch therefore complements the compact prototype boundary with instance-level normal references. Learnable Layer Fusion. Both branches produce anomaly evidence at each selected layer in Ω \Omega . For image-level detection, the patch-level abnormal probabilities are aggregated by top- k k pooling and fused with learnable layer weights: s tok ​ ( x ) \displaystyle s_{\mathrm{tok}}(x) = ∑ l ∈ Ω ω l ​ TopK r ⁡ ( a l , r det ​ ( x ) ) , \displaystyle=\sum_{l\in\Omega}\omega_{l}\operatorname{TopK}_{r}\left(a_{l,r}^{\mathrm{det}}(x)\right), (7) { ω l } l ∈ Ω \displaystyle\{\omega_{l}\}_{l\in\Omega} = softmax ⁡ ( θ ) , \displaystyle=\operatorname{softmax}(\theta), where TopK r ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \operatorname{TopK}_{r}(\cdot) averages the largest k k abnormal probabilities within each layer. The memory score is aggregated from the normalized memory distances using the same layer weights: s mem ​ ( x ) = ∑ l ∈ Ω ω l ​ TopK r ⁡ ( d ¯ l , r det ​ ( x ) ) . s_{\mathrm{mem}}(x)=\sum_{l\in\Omega}\omega_{l}\operatorname{TopK}_{r}\left(\bar{d}_{l,r}^{\mathrm{det}}(x)\right). (8) For localization, the patch-level abnormal probabilities and normalized memory distances from the segmentation branch are reshaped into 2D maps, upsampled to the input resolution, and fused with segmentation-specific layer weights to obtain A tok ​ ( x ) A_{\mathrm{tok}}(x) and A mem ​ ( x ) A_{\mathrm{mem}}(x) . Branch Fusion and Inference.

In the few-shot setting, the prototype and memory predictions are fused as s ​ ( x ) = ( 1 − λ ) ​ s tok ​ ( x ) + λ ​ s mem ​ ( x ) , s(x)=(1-\lambda)s_{\mathrm{tok}}(x)+\lambda s_{\mathrm{mem}}(x), (9) where λ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \lambda\in[0,1] balances the two branches and is set to 0.5 0.5 by default. In the zero-shot setting, no memory is constructed, and prediction reduces to the prototype branch with λ = 0 \lambda=0 . The pixel-level anomaly map A ​ ( x ) A(x) is fused analogously from A tok ​ ( x ) A_{\mathrm{tok}}(x) and A mem ​ ( x ) A_{\mathrm{mem}}(x) . 3.5 Training Objectives ReCAP is optimized on the source domains 𝒟 src \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{src}} in the zero-shot setting or on the target-domain support set 𝒮 \mathcal{S} in the few-shot setting. The training objective contains three terms: a pixel-level localization loss when lesion masks are available, an image-level detection loss, and a prototype separation regularizer. The first two losses supervise the task-specific scoring functions, while the separation regularizer keeps the base normal/abnormal prototypes discriminative before input-specific re-centering. Pixel-level Localization and Image-level Detection. For a training sample ( x i , y i , m i ) (x_{i},y_{i},m_{i}) , when the lesion mask m i m_{i} is available, the predicted anomaly map 𝐀 ​ ( x i ) \mathbf{A}(x_{i}) is supervised by a focal-plus-Dice loss: ℒ seg = ℒ focal ​ ( 𝐀 ​ ( x i ) , m i ) + ℒ dice ​ ( 𝐀 ​ ( x i ) , m i ) . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{seg}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{focal}}\big(\mathbf{A}(x_{i}),m_{i}\big)+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dice}}\big(\mathbf{A}(x_{i}),m_{i}\big). (10) This loss encourages high anomaly responses on lesion regions and suppresses activations on normal tissues. For image-level detection, the anomaly score s ​ ( x i ) s(x_{i}) is supervised by binary cross-entropy: ℒ det = BCEWithLogits ⁡ ( logit ⁡ ( s ​ ( x i ) ) , y i ) .

\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{det}}=\operatorname{BCEWithLogits}\left(\operatorname{logit}(s(x_{i})),y_{i}\right). (11) This objective trains the detection branch to separate normal and abnormal images under the same scoring function used at inference. Prototype Separation Regularization. Since conditional modulation re-centers an existing normal/abnormal boundary, the base prototypes should remain discriminative before adaptation. We therefore enforce a margin between the normal and abnormal prototypes in each branch and layer: ℒ sep = 1 2 ​ | Ω | ​ ∑ b ∈ { seg , det } ∑ l ∈ Ω max ⁡ ( 0 , cos ⁡ ( q l b , n , q l b , a ) − δ ) , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sep}}=\frac{1}{2|\Omega|}\sum_{b\in\{\mathrm{seg},\mathrm{det}\}}\sum_{l\in\Omega}\max\big(0,\cos(q_{l}^{b,n},q_{l}^{b,a})-\delta\big), (12) where δ \delta is the separation margin. This regularizer is coupled with bounded modulation: the margin preserves a discriminative base boundary, while the modulation bound allows the boundary to shift toward the current input without collapsing onto lesion-contaminated context. Overall Loss Function. The final training objective is: ℒ = ℒ seg + ℒ det + λ sep ​ ℒ sep . \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{seg}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{det}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{sep}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sep}}. (13) For datasets without pixel-level annotations, ℒ seg \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{seg}} is omitted, and ReCAP is trained with image-level supervision and prototype separation.

Following prior medical anomaly detection benchmarks (Huang et al. 2024 ) , we evaluate ReCAP on six datasets spanning five imaging domains. These include BrainMRI for brain MRI (Baid et al. 2021 ; Bakas et al. 2017 ; Menze et al. 2014 ) , LiverCT for liver CT (Bilic et al. 2023 ; Landman et al. 2015 ) , RESC and OCT17 for retinal OCT (Kermany et al. 2018 ; Hu et al. 2019 ) , ChestXray for chest X-ray (Wang et al. 2017 ) , and HIS for digital histopathology (Ehteshami Bejnordi et al. 2017 ) . BrainMRI, LiverCT, and RESC contain pixel-level annotations and are evaluated for both anomaly classification (AC) and anomaly segmentation (AS); the remaining datasets are evaluated for AC only. Dataset statistics and preprocessing details are provided in Appendix C . Competing Methods and Baselines. We compare ReCAP with representative medical anomaly detection methods, including DRA (Ding et al. 2022 ) , APRIL-GAN (Chen et al. 2023 ) , MediCLIP (Zhang et al. 2024 ) , MVFA (Huang et al. 2024 ) , MadCLIP (Shiri et al. 2025 ) , and VisualAD (Hou et al. 2026 ) . For fair comparison, all methods are evaluated under the same dataset splits, support-shot settings, and image-level or pixel-level evaluation protocols whenever applicable. For all few-shot experiments, every method uses the same predefined support indices for each dataset and shot setting. Evaluation Metrics. For anomaly classification (AC), we report image-level AUROC, the maximum F 1 F_{1} score across decision thresholds ( F 1 F_{1} -max), and average precision (AP). For anomaly segmentation (AS), we use pixel-level AUROC, pixel-level F 1 F_{1} -max, and per-region overlap (PRO). All metrics are reported as percentages. Implementation Details.

ReCAP uses a frozen CLIP ViT-L/14@336px visual encoder with lightweight segmentation and detection adapters. Images are resized to 240 × 240 240\times 240 , and patch tokens from layers { 6 , 12 , 18 , 24 } \{6,12,18,24\} are used for multi-level anomaly scoring. Only the adapters, visual prototypes, conditioning modules, and layer-fusion weights are trainable. Training combines image-level detection, pixel-level localization when masks are available, and prototype separation. All values are reported in percentage. Quantitative Comparison. Table 1 compares ReCAP with representative few-shot anomaly detection methods under low-shot settings ( K = 2 , 4 K=2,4 ). Under K = 2 K=2 , ReCAP achieves the best image-level AUROC on all six datasets. In particular, it improves the LiverCT AUROC from 84.48 % 84.48\% with MadCLIP to 90.45 % 90.45\% . For pixel-level segmentation, ReCAP achieves the best AUROC on LiverCT and RESC, reaching 99.64 % 99.64\% and 98.37 % 98.37\% , respectively, while obtaining the best F 1 F_{1} -max on all three segmentation datasets. Under K = 4 K=4 , ReCAP maintains the best image-level AUROC on five of six datasets and the best pixel-level AUROC on LiverCT and RESC. It also achieves the best pixel-level F 1 F_{1} -max on all three datasets. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of ReCAP for both anomaly classification and localization with limited target-domain supervision. Table 2 reports zero-shot results on six medical datasets. Without using target-domain support samples, ReCAP achieves the best image-level AUROC on all six datasets, outperforming both prompt-based CLIP methods and the language-free VisualAD baseline. Notable improvements include an increase from 75.26 % 75.26\% with MadCLIP to 78.40 % 78.40\% on Chest and from 95.40 % 95.40\% with MVFA to 96.58 % 96.58\% on OCT17.

For pixel-level segmentation, ReCAP achieves the best AUROC and F 1 F_{1} -max on all three segmentation datasets. These results demonstrate that the proposed language-free conditional prototypes generalize effectively to unseen medical domains while retaining accurate anomaly localization. Appendix E further reports results for K = 8 , 16 K=8,16 and provides mean ± \pm std AUROC over five random seeds for all shot settings ( K = 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 K=2,4,8,16 ), showing that the improvements are robust to random variation. Qualitative Comparison. Figure 2 compares anomaly localization results on BrainMRI, LiverCT, and retinal OCT images. APRIL-GAN produces diffuse heatmaps that extend substantially into normal regions. MVFA and MadCLIP yield more localized responses but occasionally show incomplete lesion coverage or off-target activations, while VisualAD incorrectly highlights normal anatomical structures in several BrainMRI examples. In contrast, ReCAP produces more compact anomaly responses that are visually better aligned with the annotated lesions and exhibit fewer background activations across the three modalities. These results qualitatively support the localization performance reported in our quantitative evaluation. Additional visualizations are provided in Appendix F . Anomaly Score Distribution Analysis. Figure 3 shows representative image-level score distributions on OCT17, RESC, BrainMRI, and LiverCT, with the other two datasets reported in Appendix F . ReCAP assigns low scores to most normal samples and high scores to abnormal samples. The separation is particularly clear on OCT17, RESC, and BrainMRI, demonstrating well-separated anomaly responses across retinal and brain imaging domains. Although the distributions partially overlap on the more challenging LiverCT dataset, abnormal samples remain concentrated toward higher scores. Table 3 compares model complexity and inference latency under the same input resolution, hardware, and measurement protocol. ReCAP achieves the fastest inference in both zero-shot and four-shot settings, requiring only 17.4 ms and 19.0 ms per image, respectively. The comparison with VisualAD is especially informative because both methods are language-free and use the same ViT-L/14@336px backbone. ReCAP is approximately 3.8 × 3.8\times faster in zero-shot inference ( 17.4 17.4 vs. 66.1 66.1 ms) and 3.5 × 3.5\times faster in the four-shot setting ( 19.0 19.0 vs. 65.8 65.8 ms), while using fewer method-specific parameters ( 22.0 22.0 M vs. 31.5 31.5 M). This efficiency gain stems from the different inference designs: VisualAD propagates learnable normal and abnormal tokens through multi-layer token–patch interactions and additional spatial recalibration modules, whereas ReCAP performs lightweight bounded prototype modulation followed by direct patch–prototype cosine scoring. Compared with prompt-based methods, ReCAP further avoids text encoding and image–text matching. This makes ReCAP more suitable for time-sensitive clinical screening workflows. Table 4 evaluates the contributions of the normal memory bank (MB), context-conditioning module (CCM), and learnable layer fusion (LF). The full model achieves the best AC and AS on both datasets, indicating that all three components contribute to the final performance. On LiverCT, removing LF produces the largest reductions, decreasing AC and AS by 4.00 4.00 and 2.89 2.89 percentage points, respectively, which demonstrates the importance of aggregating anomaly evidence across multiple layers. Removing MB reduces AC and AS by 2.36 2.36 and 2.72 2.72 points, while removing CCM results in drops of 1.60 1.60 and 1.48 1.48 points. On RESC, every component removal also degrades both metrics, although the margins are smaller because performance is already close to saturation.

Overall, the results support the joint use of target-domain normal references, context-conditioned prototypes, and multi-layer score fusion. AC and AS are reported as AUROC (%). Effect of Controlled Prototype Conditioning. Table 5 compares different language-free prototype designs. Static prototypes outperform the VisualAD-style anchors on all eight metrics, showing the benefit of ReCAP’s normal/abnormal prototype representation even without query conditioning. However, these prototypes remain identical for all query images and cannot adapt to anatomy-dependent appearance variations. Adding an unbounded context residual decreases all four zero-shot metrics and produces mixed results under the 4-shot setting, indicating that unconstrained modulation does not reliably improve the anomaly reference. Bounding the residual improves six of eight metrics over its unbounded counterpart, including all AC and RESC results. Introducing the gate further improves every metric, with the bounded gated residual achieving the best AC and AS across both datasets and shot settings. These results support the use of controlled query-conditioned modulation rather than either static or unconstrained anomaly prototypes. Following prior medical anomaly detection benchmarks (Huang et al. 2024 ) , we evaluate ReCAP on six datasets spanning five imaging domains. These include BrainMRI for brain MRI (Baid et al. 2021 ; Bakas et al. 2017 ; Menze et al. 2014 ) , LiverCT for liver CT (Bilic et al. 2023 ; Landman et al. 2015 ) , RESC and OCT17 for retinal OCT (Kermany et al. 2018 ; Hu et al. 2019 ) , ChestXray for chest X-ray (Wang et al. 2017 ) , and HIS for digital histopathology (Ehteshami Bejnordi et al. 2017 ) . BrainMRI, LiverCT, and RESC contain pixel-level annotations and are evaluated for both anomaly classification (AC) and anomaly segmentation (AS); the remaining datasets are evaluated for AC only. We compare ReCAP with representative medical anomaly detection methods, including DRA (Ding et al. 2022 ) , APRIL-GAN (Chen et al. 2023 ) , MediCLIP (Zhang et al. 2024 ) , MVFA (Huang et al. 2024 ) , MadCLIP (Shiri et al. 2025 ) , and VisualAD (Hou et al. 2026 ) . ReCAP uses a frozen CLIP ViT-L/14@336px visual encoder with lightweight segmentation and detection adapters. Images are resized to 240 × 240 240\times 240 , and patch tokens from layers { 6 , 12 , 18 , 24 } \{6,12,18,24\} are used for multi-level anomaly scoring. Only the adapters, visual prototypes, conditioning modules, and layer-fusion weights are trainable. Training combines image-level detection, pixel-level localization when masks are available, and prototype separation. Complete optimization settings, support protocols, augmentation, and computing resources are listed in Appendix D . Datasets. The first two variants omit query conditioning: VisualAD-style uses shared learnable anchors, whereas Static prototypes use ReCAP’s normal/abnormal prototypes. 5 Conclusion This paper presented ReCAP, a language-free framework for zero- and few-shot medical anomaly detection. ReCAP replaces static visual anchors with input-conditioned normal/abnormal prototypes whose updates are bounded and gated to provide adaptive anomaly references. For few-shot transfer, it further combines a normal-reference memory with learnable multi-layer fusion to capture target-domain normal variation and aggregate complementary anomaly cues. Across six medical datasets, ReCAP achieves the best zero-shot image-level AUROC on all six datasets and pixel-level AUROC on all three segmentation datasets, while maintaining strong performance across few-shot settings. Ablation studies confirm the contributions of controlled prototype conditioning, normal-reference memory, and layer fusion, and the efficiency analysis demonstrates fast inference without text prompts. These results establish controlled visual prototype adaptation as an effective alternative to text-based anomaly modeling. Current evaluation focuses on 2D image-based benchmarks; extending ReCAP to volumetric and multimodal clinical data remains an important direction. Appendix C Details of Medical Anomaly Detection Datasets We evaluate ReCAP on six medical anomaly detection datasets covering diverse modalities, anatomical regions, and evaluation settings. As summarized in Table 6 , BrainMRI, LiverCT, and RESC provide both image-level anomaly classification (AC) and pixel-level anomaly segmentation (AS) annotations, whereas OCT17, Chest, and HIS are evaluated for image-level anomaly classification only. The labeled pool is used only for source-domain training or few-shot support construction, depending on the evaluation protocol, while the test split is kept fixed for evaluation. Normal-only training splits provided by some datasets are not used under our few-shot or zero-shot protocols. To avoid patient-level leakage, samples from the same patient are assigned to the same split whenever patient/case identifiers are available. For datasets without exposed patient identifiers, we follow the official benchmark splits and do not mix samples across the labeled pool and test set. BrainMRI. The BrainMRI dataset is derived from BraTS2021 (Baid et al. 2021 ; Bakas et al. 2017 ; Menze et al. 2014 ) and uses FLAIR volumes for brain anomaly detection. We extract 2D slices from selected depth ranges of the original 3D volumes and resize them to 240 × 240 240\times 240 . The benchmark contains 83 labeled pool samples and 3,715 test images for evaluating both anomaly classification and localization. LiverCT. The LiverCT dataset is constructed from abdominal CT scans, where normal samples are taken from BTCV (Landman et al. 2015 ) and abnormal testing samples are obtained from LiTS (Bilic et al. 2023 ) . The CT volumes are converted into grayscale images using an abdominal window and then cropped into 2D axial slices. The benchmark includes 166 labeled pool samples and 1,493 test slices. Since pixel-level lesion annotations are available, LiverCT is used for both AC and AS evaluation. RESC.

RESC is a retinal OCT dataset designed for retinal edema analysis. It provides pixel-level annotations of abnormal regions, making it suitable for both image-level and pixel-level anomaly detection. The benchmark includes 115 labeled pool samples and 1,805 test images, with an original image size of 512 × 1024 512\times 1024 . OCT17. OCT17 is a retinal OCT dataset mainly used for image-level anomaly classification. It contains normal OCT images and multiple abnormal retinal disease categories. The benchmark includes 32 labeled pool samples and 968 test images, with an image size of 512 × 496 512\times 496 . Chest. The Chest dataset is based on RSNA chest radiographs (Wang et al. 2017 ; Shih et al. 2019 ) , where abnormal cases are associated with lung opacity or other non-normal findings. The benchmark includes 1,490 labeled pool samples and 17,194 test images. This dataset is evaluated under the image-level anomaly classification setting. HIS. The HIS dataset is constructed from Camelyon16 (Ehteshami Bejnordi et al. 2017 ) , which consists of hematoxylin and eosin stained histopathology whole-slide images of lymph node tissue. Following the patch-based setting, normal and abnormal image patches are extracted from the original WSIs. The benchmark includes 236 labeled pool samples and 2,000 test patches, and is used for image-level anomaly classification.
